sources.source: General guidelines for secondary indexes in DynamoDB (AWS documentation)

items.item: a global secondary index is considered global because queries on it can span all of the data in the base table, across all partitions
a local secondary index is local because every one of its partitions is scoped to a base table partition sharing the same partition key value

A celebrity key isn't a sign the shard key was chosen badly in the usual sense — any shard key, however high its overall cardinality, can have one value that drives a disproportionate share of traffic; cardinality and traffic skew are independent properties of a workload.

Salting only works because it targets the symptom at exactly the key that has it — splitting every key into salted sub-keys would fix nothing (it would just multiply the key count) while still leaving other keys' own relative traffic shares unchanged.

A local secondary index's cost advantage is conditional, not unconditional: it only pays off when the query already supplies the base table's partition key; a query on a different attribute, without that key, degrades to exactly the cost of no index at all.

A global secondary index's own partitions can themselves develop a celebrity-key problem, independent of the base table's — if one indexed attribute value (e.g. one status) dominates query traffic, the fix is the identical salting technique applied to the GSI's own key, not a base-table change.

The write-pause window a correct resharding operation pays for isn't a performance accident to be optimized away — it's the only way every writer can agree on the new key-range boundary at the same logical instant; a 'faster' reshard that skips it trades correctness for speed, not just UX for speed.

Vitess's own documented cutover (making the source read-only while the target catches up) and CockroachDB's own range split (a new Raft group spun up for the new range) solve the identical membership-agreement problem through different mechanisms — a pause-then-switch versus a new consensus group taking over mid-flight.

items.item: DynamoDB's adaptive capacity automates exactly the salting decision this topic's own examples.py makes by hand — the system detects a hot item and isolates it onto its own partition automatically, without an engineer having to notice the celebrity key first.

items.item: Choosing a shard key from access patterns rather than cardinality alone means asking which queries need to land on one shard (a tenant's own data, a user's own timeline) before asking which key has the most distinct values — the two criteria can point to different keys entirely.

This topic's own executable claims isolate the celebrity-key effect cleanly by giving one key a fixed, large traffic share and splitting the remainder evenly among the rest, rather than a smooth Zipf curve, specifically so the salting fix's effect is measurable and not confounded by a second- or third-ranked heavy key landing on the same shard by chance.

This topic's own 'Prove it' answer generalizes topic 21's 'adding nodes doesn't fix a hot tail' result: no amount of key-space cardinality fixes a celebrity key, because the fix has to target the specific key driving the skew, not the shard count or the hashing scheme everyone else's data already sits under.
